Renewals — Failed Payment Recovery Playbook
A different kind of call from every other playbook in this hub. These people are not
leads — they are active Standard Meds patients whose subscription renewal was
declined by their bank. Nothing needs to be sold. A working card has to be put on
file.
QUEUE APPLIES TO GOAL DISPOSITION
ReFlow → Renewals All verticals Update the card on file Recovered
Executive Summary
01
Every other playbook in this hub is about someone who almost became a patient. This one is
about someone who already is one. They completed the assessment, were approved by a
physician, received their medication, and have been on a recurring subscription — and then, at
renewal time, their card was declined.
Page 1 of 17

THE WHOLE JOB IN ONE SENTENCE
The subscription is still alive — it was never cancelled. Nobody has to be re-sold, re-approved
or re-prescribed. You put a working card on file and the treatment continues. That is the
entire call.
WHY THIS IS THE BEST-CONVERTING LIST YOU WILL EVER CALL FOR US
The person on the other end chose this product, paid for it at least once, and in most cases is
still taking it. They usually don't know the payment failed — the bank declined it silently and the
shipment simply stopped. You are not interrupting a stranger with an offer; you are calling a
customer about a billing problem that is already costing them their treatment. Expect a far
warmer reception than any funnel-recovery call.
NOBODY IN THIS QUEUE CHOSE TO CANCEL
The list is filtered on purpose: it contains card declines only. Customers who deliberately
cancelled their subscription are excluded and must never be called from here. If someone on
the call tells you they cancelled on purpose, respect it immediately, mark the disposition, and
end the call politely — do not talk them out of it.
What actually happened, in plain terms
1. The patient's subscription reached its renewal date and Standard Meds attempted the
charge.
2. The bank that issued the card refused it — expired card, no funds, a reissued number after
a lost or stolen card, or a generic refusal that the bank won't explain.
3. The charge failed, so the refill was not produced or shipped. In most cases no email or text
reached the patient, or it went unread. From their side, the box just stopped arriving.
4. Their name lands in the Renewals tab in ReFlow, with the failure reason, the plan, the
amount and how many days it has been overdue.
How this call differs from a recovery call
You stay on the line and fix it together. You keep the patient on the phone and update the
card with them, during the call. The call is only finished when the new card is saved and the
confirmation shows on screen.
There is no offer, no plan to pick, no discount conversation. The plan and the price are
already agreed. You are restoring an existing arrangement.
Time matters more. Every week the card stays broken is a week the patient goes without
medication — and the longer the gap, the more likely they simply stop.
Page 2 of 17

You handle payment data. That brings its own hard rules — see §7.
The Queue at a Glance
02
Where the list lives, who is on it, and what each row is telling you before you dial.
ReFlow → Renewals
RETENTION QUEUE · ALL VERTICALS · ONE ROW PER CUSTOMER
A dedicated tab in ReFlow, separate from the funnel-recovery lists. It is built from Standard Meds'
own billing records, so everything on the row is the real state of that person's subscription — not a
guess.
WHO'S ON IT Active subscribers whose renewal charge was declined by the card. Deliberate
cancellations are excluded by design.
ONE ROW EACH One line per customer, not per failed charge. If the same person's card failed
three times, you see them once.
PRODUCT Which brand and plan they are on — NeuroCalmRx, LiftRx, QuattroRx, TriShot,
ZoliraRx, NAD+ Therapy. It is a column, not a tab: you may get any vertical in the
same shift, so check it before you open your mouth.
AMOUNT & PLAN The exact renewal that failed — the number you should be ready to say out loud
if asked.
DAYS OVERDUE How long the renewal has been sitting unpaid. Highlighted from 14 days, red
from 30. Work the fresh ones first — they are the easiest saves.
DECLINE REASON The wording the bank gave for the refusal. Read §3 before you interpret it.
SUBSCRIPTION The live billing state. Most rows read RECYCLE_FAILED , which means the system
STATUS is still retrying — the subscription is intact and a new card fixes it immediately.
UPDATE THE The drawer gives you a direct "Open the order in Dosable" link. That is where
CARD the card gets changed — full walkthrough in §5.
NOTES Shared with the whole operation. Log what happened on every call — but never
the card number (§7).
THE LIST REFRESHES ON A DELAY — ALWAYS ASSUME IT MAY BE STALE
Page 3 of 17

Billing data is pulled in on a cycle rather than live, so a customer can already have fixed their
card in the meantime. Never open with "your payment failed" as an accusation. Open by
confirming, and if they say it is already sorted, thank them, verify in the drawer, and disposition
accordingly.
WHEN NO ORDER LINK IS AVAILABLE
A few rows show no resolvable Dosable order. Those customers are not skipped — the drawer
gives you their CheckoutChamp customer id and their email so you can find them by hand.
These are exactly the people nobody has been calling, so they are worth the extra minute.
Dispositions — what to set when the call ends
Same six statuses you already use on the funnel queues. There is nothing new to learn:
Recovered
The new card was saved and went through. This is the win — set it as soon as the update is confirmed on
screen.
Callback scheduled
They want to handle it later, or the cardholder isn't the person you reached. Agree a time and set this.
Didn't reply
No answer, voicemail, or no contact made on this attempt.
Not interested
They no longer want the subscription. Respect it — no rebuttal loop, no second pitch.
Organic
They had already fixed the card themselves before you called.
Lost
Unreachable, wrong number, or the account cannot be restored.
Why the Card Failed — and What It Means for the Call
03
The reason on the row comes from the customer's own bank, passed through the payment
processor untouched. Standard Meds does not decide it and does not score anybody for fraud.
Page 4 of 17

Read it as what the bank said, nothing more.

THE LABEL IS ONLY TRUSTWORTHY IN ONE DIRECTION
"Do Not Honor" and "Generic Decline" are exactly the wildcards banks use when they will not
reveal the real reason — which can include loss, theft or a fraud flag. So the absence of a
fraud-sounding label proves nothing, and its presence is only the bank's version. Never
Page 5 of 17

present a decline reason to the customer as a fact about them. Present it as "the bank didn't
approve it."
COUNTER-INTUITIVE BUT TRUE — "LOST" AND "STOLEN" ARE THE WARMEST CALLS HERE
It reads like bad news and it is the opposite. A cancelled-and-reissued card means the
customer is still a customer, still has a working card in their wallet, and the only thing standing
between them and their next shipment is a number they never got around to updating.
The Call Playbook
04
One stage, one card. Openers and questions are a guide, not a script to read verbatim — adjust
to your own voice. Remember who you are calling: a paying patient, mid-treatment, who almost
certainly does not know anything went wrong.
RENEWALS · SINGLE STAGE
Renewal Declined — Card Update
An existing patient whose renewal charge was refused by their bank. Their next shipment is on
hold. They are not expecting your call and, in most cases, have no idea there is a problem. Your
tone is service, not sales: you are calling to keep their treatment from being interrupted, and
the fix takes two minutes.
GOAL
New card saved & confirmed
AVG CALL
≤ 5 min
POSTURE
Service — never accusatory
BEFORE YOU DIAL (10 SECONDS IN THE DRAWER)
Which product are they on — you must name it correctly.
The amount and the plan that failed.
The decline reason, so you know which version of the conversation you are in (§3).
Days overdue — a 9-day gap and a 60-day gap are different calls.
Any notes from a previous attempt.
Page 6 of 17

OPENER (≤ 20 SEC)
"Hi {first name}, this is {agent name} calling from Standard Meds about your {product}
subscription. Nothing's wrong with your account — your last renewal didn't go through on
the card we have on file, so your refill is on hold. It's a two-minute fix. Is this a good time?"
FRAME IT (≤ 30 SEC)
"Your bank declined the charge on {date} — that happens for all sorts of reasons, most of
them nothing to do with you. Your subscription is still active, I just need to get a working
card on file and your next shipment goes straight out."
DISCOVERY — ONLY IF YOU NEED IT
"Has your card changed recently — new one from the bank, or a new expiry date?"
Most of the time this single question ends the diagnosis. If they say yes, you are already
at the close.
ADDRESS — MOST COMMON PATTERNS
"I didn't know anything failed." → the normal case. "That's exactly why I'm calling
— the bank doesn't always tell you either. Let's get it sorted now."
"I already updated my card." → thank them, check the drawer, and confirm the
charge went through. If the row is stale, disposition as Organic. Never argue with the
customer about their own bank.
"Did you take the money anyway?" → no. A declined charge means nothing was
taken. Say it plainly; this fear ends the call if you leave it hanging.
"I don't want to give my card over the phone." → completely reasonable. Do not
push. Walk them through the self-service route in the Patient Portal instead (§5b) —
ideally while they're still on the line with you. If they'd rather do it later, agree a time
and set Callback scheduled.
"I want to stop / I don't need it anymore." → one honest question about why, listen
to the answer, and if they confirm, respect it. Set Not interested and log the reason
in the notes — that feedback is worth more than a forced save.
"Can I skip this month and restart later?" → don't improvise a payment
arrangement. Offer a callback on a date they choose and note it. Their subscription
stays as it is in the meantime.
Anything clinical — a reaction, a dose question, whether they should keep taking it
→ stop. That routes to the Standard Meds medical team, never to you.
Page 7 of 17

WHY THEY SHOULD KEEP GOING (USE IT IF THEY HESITATE)
CONTINUITY ANGLES — NO DISCOUNTS, NO INVENTED OFFERS
Their price and plan are already locked in — restoring the card changes nothing about what
they agreed to
Nothing has to start over: no new assessment, no new physician review, no new prescription
These are maintenance treatments — the results come from staying consistent, and a gap
gives back progress they already paid for
Their clinical support, dose adjustments and consults all continue with the subscription
The shipment goes out as soon as the card clears — usually the same production cycle
CLOSE
"I've got the secure form open on my side — if you've got the card handy I can put
it on file right now and your refill goes out."
ACTION ON YES
Go to §5 and update the card while they are on the line. Do not end the call until the
confirmation appears on screen. Then read back what will happen: the plan, the
amount, and that their next shipment is released.
CONFIRM BEFORE HANGING UP
"All set — the new card is on file, your {product} subscription is active again, and your
refill is released. Same plan, same price, nothing else changes. Anything else I can help you
with?"
VOICEMAIL SCRIPT
"Hi {first name}, this is {agent name} from Standard Meds. I'm calling about your
subscription — the last renewal didn't go through on the card we have on file, so your refill
is on hold. Nothing's wrong with your account and it only takes a minute to fix. Please give
us a call back when you get a chance. Thank you!"
Note: never leave the product name, the medication or any health detail on a voicemail — you cannot
know who listens to it. "Your subscription" is as specific as it gets.
Updating the Card — Step by Step
05
Page 8 of 17

This is the part that closes the call. Do it with the customer on the line, and stay on the line until
the confirmation shows. There are two routes: you update it, from the "Open the order in
Dosable" link in the Renewals drawer in ReFlow (steps 1–5 below), or they update it
themselves in the Patient Portal while you guide them (§5b) — for customers who won't read a
card over the phone.
BEFORE YOU TYPE A SINGLE DIGIT
Card data has stricter rules than anything else you handle. Pause the call recording while the
number is being read to you, never write the number down or paste it into notes, and never
keep it after the update. Full rules in §7 — read them before your first call.
STEP 1
Open the order and find the payment method
The order page shows you the customer's details and the card currently on file — you
will see only the last digits and the expiry date, which is all anyone can see. Confirm you
are on the right person before continuing: name, email and the order number at the top.
The order page. The Payment Method block on the right is the card currently on file — click it to
edit.
STEP 2
Click "Update Card" in the secure card window
A window opens showing the current card and a security notice. Card changes are
processed through the payment gateway, not stored in this screen — clicking Update
Page 9 of 17

Card takes you to the secure form and brings you back here afterwards.
Edit Credit Card Information → press Update Card.
STEP 3
Enter the new card and billing address
Fill in the card number, expiry month and year, and the security code, then the billing
address exactly as it appears on the customer's statement — a mismatched ZIP code is
itself a common cause of decline. Read the card number back to the customer before
submitting, then press Update Information.
Page 10 of 17

The secure Update Payment & Billing form. Card details on top, billing address below, then
Update Information.
ASK FOR THE BILLING ADDRESS, DON'T ASSUME IT
The shipping address on the order is not always the billing address on the card — a new
card often comes with a new address. Ask: "and what's the billing address on that
card?"
STEP 4
Wait for the confirmation — then say it out loud
You are done only when the confirmation appears: "Your card information has been
securely updated in our system." If it does not appear, or an error comes back, the
card was not saved — check the digits with the customer and try again, or try a second
card. Never tell a customer they are all set based on hope.
Page 11 of 17

The confirmation you are waiting for. Only now is the call a save.
STEP 5
Go back to ReFlow and set the disposition
Return to the Renewals drawer and mark the customer as Recovered, then add a short
note about what happened on the call — for example "card reissued by bank, new card
on file, confirmation shown". The note is visible to the whole operation and is what stops
somebody calling the same person tomorrow.
RECOVERED MEANS CONFIRMED, NOT PROMISED
Only set Recovered once the confirmation has appeared on screen. If the customer
said yes but the update failed, that is a Callback scheduled, not a save. Inflating this
number costs the operation more than a missed call does.
5b · If the customer won't read their card over the phone
Some customers will not read a card number out loud, and they are right to be careful — never
push past it. There is a second route that costs you nothing: they update the card themselves
in their Patient Portal, while you stay on the line and talk them through it. The save still
happens on your call.
1. Log in to the Patient Portal — patient.standardmeds.com/login
2. Go to Profile
3. Click My Billing Information
Page 12 of 17

4. Click Edit Payment Information
5. Enter the new card details and save
STAY ON THE LINE WHILE THEY DO IT
Read the steps out one at a time and wait for them at each one. A customer who hangs up to
"do it later" usually doesn't. If they genuinely can't do it now, agree a specific time, set
Callback scheduled, and note where they got stuck.
EVEN ON THIS ROUTE, THE DISPOSITION RULE DOESN'T CHANGE
You still only mark Recovered once the update is confirmed — here that means the customer
tells you the card saved without an error. If they finished after the call ended and you never saw
it confirmed, that is a Callback scheduled until you verify.
NEVER ASK FOR THEIR PORTAL LOGIN
You are guiding them through their screen, not taking control of it. Never ask for their
password, never ask them to read anything back from the payment form, and never ask them to
share their screen or their card details "just to check". If they get stuck on the login itself, that's
a Standard Meds support matter — take a note and pass it on.
Objection Library
06
Guidance, not scripts to read verbatim. Two hard boundaries run through all of it: anything
clinical goes to the physician, and anything about the money already charged goes to Standard
Meds support — you never improvise a refund, a credit or a discount.
Q "How do I know this is really Standard Meds and not a scam?"
A "Completely fair question, and I'd rather you ask it than not. I'm calling on behalf of Standard Meds
about the {product} subscription in your name — I'm not going to ask you for a password, a social
security number or anything from your bank login. If you'd rather not read your card to me at all, you
don't have to — you can log into your own Patient Portal and update it there yourself, and I'll talk you
through where to click. Would that be easier?" (Never pressure past this. A customer protecting their
card is doing the right thing.)
Q "Did you already take the money?"
A "No. The charge was declined, which means nothing left your account — the payment never
completed. That's exactly why your refill is on hold rather than on its way."
Page 13 of 17

Q "Why didn't anyone tell me?"
A "We do send a notification, but they land in spam more often than they should — and the bank usually
doesn't tell you either. That's why we call. Let's just get it fixed."
Q "My card is fine, there's nothing wrong with it."
A "I believe you — and it may well be. Banks decline recurring charges for all sorts of reasons that have
nothing to do with your balance: a new card issued, a fraud filter, a travel block. Either way I can put the
card on file again now, or you can call your bank and I'll try it again after. Whichever you prefer."
Q "I don't have the money right now."
A "That's no problem at all, and thank you for telling me. Is there a date that works better for you? I'll
make a note and we'll pick it back up then." (Set a callback. Never offer a discount, a partial charge, or a
payment plan — those don't exist for you to give.)
Q "Can I just pay a smaller amount?" / "Can I get a discount for the trouble?"
A "I can't change the pricing on my side — what I can do is get your existing plan running again exactly
as it is, at the price you already have. If you'd like to look at a different plan, I'll pass you to the Standard
Meds team." (Hard rule: no invented offers.)
Q "I want to cancel."
A "Understood, and that's your call. Can I ask what made you decide — was it the treatment itself, the
cost, or something else?" (One question, genuine listening, then respect it. Log the reason in the notes
and set Not interested. Do not run a rebuttal loop on someone who has told you they're done.)
Q "I stopped taking it because of a side effect."
A "I'm glad you told me — that's something the medical team needs to know, and they're the right
people for it, not me. I'll flag it and someone from the clinical side can reach out. I won't put a card on file
today." (Never re-start a subscription for someone reporting an adverse reaction, and never advise them
on it.)
Q "Can you use the same card I have on file, just try it again?"
A "I can ask for it to be retried, but if the bank declined it once it usually declines it again until something
changes on their end. The quickest route is either a different card, or you call your bank to approve it and
we retry after."
Q "Is my card safe with you?"
A "The details go straight into the secure payment form — I'm not saving them anywhere, I can't see the
full number afterwards, and it isn't written down on my side."
Q "My husband/wife handles the cards — can I have them call you?"
A "Of course. I'll schedule a callback for a time that works, or they can call us back directly." (Do not
discuss the medication, the condition or the treatment with anyone other than the patient — see §7.)
Q "How soon do I get my shipment?"
Page 14 of 17

A "As soon as the card clears, your order is released and goes out on the next shipping cycle. You'll get
the tracking by email like you did before."
Q "Do I have to redo the medical questions?"
A "No — nothing starts over. Your prescription and your plan are still in place. This is purely the payment
method."
Compliance & Operational Rules
07
The universal rules from your first Standard Meds playbook still apply in full — calling window,
self-identification, recording disclosure, opt-out, no invented discounts, no claiming approval
before physician review. This section covers only what is different or elevated for renewals —
and this queue adds a category of rules the funnel queues don't have, because here you touch
payment data.
#1 RULE — THE CARD NUMBER NEVER EXISTS ANYWHERE BUT THE SECURE FORM
Pause the recording before the customer reads their card number, and resume after. Never
write it on paper, in a chat, in a ticket, in the ReFlow notes, or in any file. Never repeat the full
number back within earshot of anyone. Never ask for the security code before you are on the
payment form, and never keep it. Never photograph or screenshot a screen containing card
data. If a customer emails or texts you their card number, do not use it and report it — that is an
incident.
New or elevated for renewals
Never call a deliberate cancellation
This queue is card declines only. If someone tells you they cancelled on purpose, that is the end of the
conversation — respect it, disposition it, move on. No save attempt, no second offer.
Never accuse, never diagnose the bank
Do not tell a customer they had no money, that their card was flagged for fraud, or that their bank thinks
anything about them. The decline reason is the bank's word and it is often deliberately vague. "The bank
didn't approve it" is the only framing you need.
Never invent a payment arrangement
No discounts, no partial charges, no "I'll waive this month", no payment plans, no promises about refunds
or credits. Those are Standard Meds decisions. Offering one you can't deliver breaks the customer's trust
and the account.
Page 15 of 17

Never restart a subscription after a health complaint
If a customer reports a side effect, a reaction, or that they were told to stop — do not take a card. Note it,
flag it to Standard Meds, end the call. A save here is a safety incident, not a win.
Never discuss treatment with a third party
If a spouse, relative or assistant answers, you may say you are calling from Standard Meds about a billing
matter. You may not name the medication, the condition, or anything about their health. Ask for the
patient or offer a callback. This is a HIPAA line.
Never mark Recovered on a promise
The disposition follows the confirmation on screen, not the customer's intention. Everything else is a
callback.
Always confirm identity before anything else
Name and email on the order, at minimum, before you discuss the subscription. You are calling about
somebody's medication and their money — being on the wrong call is the worst outcome available.
Always offer the self-service route
A customer who doesn't want to read a card over the phone is being sensible. Walk them through the
Patient Portal steps in §5b instead — offer it before you lose the save, and stay on the line while they do it.
Always log the call in the notes
What happened, what was agreed, when to call back — never the card details. The notes are shared, and
they're the only thing that stops a customer being called twice about the same problem.
Lead with service, not with the sale
These are paying patients mid-treatment. The reason to fix the card is that their treatment shouldn't be
interrupted. Sell nothing else on this call — no upsells, no plan changes, no add-ons.
IF ANYTHING GOES SIDEWAYS, ESCALATE RATHER THAN IMPROVISE
A disputed charge, a chargeback, a customer claiming they were billed after cancelling, a
duplicate charge, an angry call about money — all of these go to Standard Meds. Take the
details, tell the customer it is being passed on, and log it in the notes. Do not negotiate, do not
promise an outcome, and do not defend a charge you cannot see the full history of.
